catalog_quote: 2.13. Tone and stress. There are at least two distinctive tones: high (marked by an accent aigu, e.g. á) and low (left unmarked). Furthermore, mid (ā), falling (â) and rising tone (ǎ) will be marked, although it is not known whether they are distinct units. Stress (ˈa) is a phoneme of its own. [p. 60, §2.6:] Sentence questions are distinguished from statements only by a rising tone and stress on the last syllable, e.g. ísí alɛ'ɛ 'he is coming' : ísí alɛ'ˈɛ̌ 'is he coming?'; damatú alɛ'ɛ́to 'the woman is coming' : damatú alɛ'ɛ́tˈǒ 'is the woman coming?'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Heine treats Yaaku as having at least a two-way lexical tone contrast (H vs L) and, separately, phonemic (contrastive, unpredictable) stress, which he marks lexically with ˈ before the stressed syllable in his transcriptions (e.g. nawˈáxan 'see', wˈaaʼ 'cows', ˈiíçeʼ 'I'); he gives no default position for word stress. The only positional statement is intonational: in yes/no questions stress (with rising tone) shifts to the last syllable of the sentence.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Heine flags the whole sketch as fragmentary (informant lost after three weeks) and says it is unknown whether mid, falling and rising tones are distinct units.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level claim (stress as a phoneme, marked per word in citation and sentence examples); the p.60 remark is sentence-level (question intonation: stress + rising tone on the sentence-final syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: Heine's data are from one speaker (Koisa Olelengai, c.45, 1970) of Yaaku as spoken in Mukogodo Forest west of Doldol, Laikipia; language names Yaaku / Mukogodo / Mogogodo / Siegu all = yaak1241 (not the Mukogodo dialect of Maasai, which is Nilotic). The language was already moribund; Heine calls the notes fragmentary.

sources.note: §2.13 'Tone and stress' (p.35): at least two distinctive tones (high, low; mid/falling/rising also marked but status unknown); 'Stress (ˈa) is a phoneme of its own.' Stress is marked lexically with ˈ in the data (e.g. nawˈáxan, wˈaaʼ). §2.6 (p.60): sentence questions differ from statements only by a rising tone and stress on the last syllable. No default stress position is stated.
